newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank prepares to amend own statutes for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank prepares to amend own statutes for EMU.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank said on Thursday it was gearing up for fundamental alterations to its own statutes to prepare for changed monetary policy structures under Europe's single currency, scheduled for launch in 1999.
A draft amendment to the central bank law had met with "full consensus" among Bundesbank council members, the bank's president Hans Tietmeyer told a news conference on Thursday.
"The provisions must be made fully compatible with the (Maastricht) Treaty," Tietmeyer said.
The move to economic and monetary union (EMU) will shift responsibility for monetary policy in the euro zone to the European Central Bank (ECB), to be established in 1998.

That will demand changes to Bundesbank law, which are due to be discussed in cabinet next week and should include the elimination of a clause giving the German government a right of veto on central bank decisions.
"Of course they (Bonn) have never used it (the veto), but it is there and it is not compatible," Tietmeyer said.
The clause in theory allows Bonn to overturn a Bundesbank monetary move for a limited period of time.

Tietmeyer, who was addressing the Bundesbank's annual news conference, also said that many more legal questions remained as to how central banks would conduct their business once the ECB takes control of EMU monetary policy
"The European Monetary Institute council will be discussing many concrete issues over the coming months. The Bundesbank will be taking part in this with great interest," he said.
Among the issues still open were the precise changes needed to annual and weekly reports issued by the Bundesbank.
Tietmeyer said the EMI had already issued guidelines for the construction of weekly reports but that the implications for annual reports, and annual accounts, were still unclear.
Such issues "can only be decided definitively by the ECB itself," Tietmeyer said.
Other questions included the level of reserves which the Bundesbank and other national central banks would be obliged to transfer to the ECB.
It is expected that the ECB will have around 50 billion marks in foreign exchange reserves, although that figure depends on all 15 EU countries taking part in EMU from the outset, Tietmeyer said.
Asked whether gold reserves would be transferred to the ECB, Tietmeyer said: "Whether gold reserves will be transferred and if yes, to what extent, is still completely open."
The Bundesbank chief also reaffirmed his belief that gold sales should not take place.
"We in principle believe that gold sales should not take place, that is also true of our position relative to the International Monetary Fund," Tietmeyer said.

For the time being, however, Tietmeyer said there was unlikely to be any major change in the Bundesbank's mode of operation, especially given the huge volume of work the euro preparations had created.
Tietmeyer said the Bundesbank's organisational structure, with its hierarchy of policy-making council, directorate and regional state divisions, should remain intact.

While the Bundesbank would continue to gradually streamline its branch network, from 167 branches at end-1996 towards its target of 128 branches, such changes were not yet directly related to preparations for the ECB.
